source.title: Differential Transformer
source.authors: Tianzhu Ye; Li Dong; Yuqing Xia; Yutao Sun; Yi Zhu; Gao Huang; Fu-Ru Wei

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The study runs parameter-count and training-token sweeps and measures language-model validation loss, directly testing the scaling relationship with the same general measurement as the original scaling-law work, on a different architecture.
record.gate_note: The scaling figures and their fitted curves bear on V1. Downstream-task comparisons, long-context results, and other evaluations are not rows for V6 because the paper does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss. No compute-optimal allocation sweep is reported.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper. It fits Kaplan-style curves only to compare DIFF Transformer with Transformer at matched loss. Its sole statement on the law is one sentence: 'The scaling law (Kaplan et al., 2020) empirically fits well'. No exponents, fit quality or residuals are reported, and no point values are given. The reported results are the method's efficiency gains (62.2%, 59.5%, 63.7%), so the scaling law serves as a tool, not as the object of test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that DIFF Transformer needs about 65% of the model size or training tokens to match Transformer loss: 62.2% and 59.5% of parameters and 63.7% of tokens, per the fitted curves. They also say it outperforms Transformer on long context, retrieval, hallucination, in-context learning and activation outliers.
record.recipe_differences: Uses model-size and training-token sweeps and validation-loss curves, but compares a differential-attention architecture against Transformer rather than reproducing the original study's full setup; the paper does not state fitted exponents.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports relative robustness to different λ initialization strategies in an ablation, but this is not a test of scaling-law fit sensitivity.
record.problems: The scaling-curve point values and uncertainty are not reported in the text; values are only plotted. The parameter and token sweeps cover less than several orders of magnitude, and there is no compute-optimal allocation experiment.
record.rows_left_out: No reported parameter-sweep or token-sweep checkpoints were left out; the figures do not provide point values in the text, so individual plotted observations are recorded as figure only.

untested.parts: No exponents, fit statistics or loss values. Ranges are about 1.2 decades in parameters (830M–13.1B, 10B tokens each) and about 1 decade in tokens (checkpoints of one 3B run). There is no compute axis.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 'supports' label rested on a single unquantified sentence that the Kaplan law 'fits well'. That is too thin for a verdict; at most it is weak qualitative consistency with V1 over about one decade. The reader's 'limits_scope' label confused untested range with a scope limitation. If a curator prefers to treat it as a test, it is at most a weak T3 'supports' for V1 on LLaMA-style and differential-attention models, with no numbers. The ablation (Table 6) varies head count and dimension at 1.4B (3.087 vs 3.088 loss), a tiny shape change. It is not a systematic V4 test.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests parameter-count and token-count scaling, but not compute scaling, whether the other axes are non-bottlenecks, or the claim over several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fit is explicitly tested as a prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute optimization over parameter and token allocation is reported.
The study does not systematically vary depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
Math fine-tuning and distillation results are not tests of whether the same power-law form holds in other training regimes.
Downstream evaluations compare models, but do not test predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not test dependence of exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, nor report systematic bending away from a power law.
